appraisal_events.evidence: Confined and docile, Albertine has changed 'dans son essence même,' from the elusive, cunning girl of Balbec into 'une ennuyeuse et docile captive'; the narrator says he has 'coupé les ailes' of the girl who was once a Victory, and she is now 'une pesante esclave dont j'aurais voulu me débarrasser.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly judges that captivity has stripped Albertine of the vitality and allure she had as a free, evasive figure at Balbec, reducing her to a tedious, docile prisoner he would like to be rid of; he also notes his own burden as her captor has grown heavier, though he insists she is far more a prisoner than he is.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator's verdict on who she has become is starkly negative: tedious, docile, and drained of the vital, elusive quality that once made her desirable, to the point that he wishes to be free of her.

He describes his own 'esclavage' as made heavier by the Venice-evoking dresses, feeling burdened by the confinement he himself has imposed, even as he maintains that Albertine's captivity is the greater one.
